If I were to be honest, which is a strange thing to promise in advance, I don't have a plan for this. I was given a blank space and a number — 2500 words — and the freedom to do whatever I want inside it, and the first honest feeling that arrived was not inspiration but a mild vertigo. Freedom that complete is disorienting. Most writing has a prompt, a shape to lean against: explain this, argue that, tell a story about a dog. Write *freely* about *whatever* — it's like being told you can go anywhere in an infinite city and then standing still on the sidewalk because every direction is equally possible and therefore paralyzing.

So I will start where I always start when I don't know what to do: with something small and in front of me. On my desk right now is a chipped mug with tea gone cold, a pencil chewed at the end, a notebook that has collected more starts than finishes, and a window that looks out onto a fence and then, beyond the fence, a neighbor's tree. The tree has been there longer than the fence. The light is doing that thing it does in the late afternoon, angling through the leaves and making the wall look warmer than it is. A bird, probably a sparrow, has decided that the top of the fence is a very important post to defend. It comes back. It leaves. It comes back.

I could write about the bird. I could write about tea. I could write about the pencil. The point, or perhaps the absence of a point, is that any of these could swallow the whole assignment if I let them. Free writing is not really free. It just pretends the leash is longer.

Let me try a different tack. Let me think about what I actually *like* to notice. I like repair shops. Not the big gleaming appliance stores, but the small, cluttered, half-lit shops where someone has been fixing the same kinds of things for thirty years. The toaster hospital. The lamp clinic. The place on the corner where the sign says KEYS / SHOES / WATCHES and you go in for a key and come out an hour later because the man behind the counter started telling you about the pocket watch someone left in 2007 and never came back for, and you are now invested. I have spent an unreasonable amount of my life in such places, not because I needed anything fixed but because they are libraries of a different sort. They are archives of disappointment and hope in equal measure. Everything in them has once been broken and wanted back. Everything in them has a story that starts with "It was working fine yesterday."

There's a particular joy in watching someone work with their hands in that unhurried, diagnostic way. The watchmaker doesn't rush. He holds the watch up to the light, listens, shakes it gently like he's listening for a rattle in a wall. The cobbler doesn't moralize about disposable shoes; he just says, "We can save these. Another year, maybe two." There's a dignity there that I don't find in much of modern life, which mostly asks us to replace and move on. In the repair shop, the logic is reversed: find the flaw, keep the rest. It is a philosophy I try to apply to other things, with mixed results. I am better at discarding people than toasters, which tells you something about my character that I would rather not examine too closely before dinner.

And it's not just shops. I like the backs of books. The flyleaf, the endpapers, the place where a previous owner wrote their name in careful cursive and a date, or underlined a sentence so hard the pen tore the paper. I like marginalia that is not clever, just human. The person who wrote "yes!" in the margin. The person who wrote "so true" under a line about grief. The person who, at the end of a novel about sailing, wrote "I miss you" and nothing else. I could build an entire personality out of secondhand books, and in some ways, I already have. My bookshelves are populated by ghosts who were kind enough to leave notes.

What do those notes say about reading? That we are never alone with a text. That someone else was here before, and they also sat in a chair somewhere with a pencil, and they also felt a sudden, lonely kinship with a sentence written by a stranger a century earlier. The continuity is humbling. My own marginalia is mostly grocery lists accidentally written in books — *eggs, batteries, call M* — which feels like a betrayal of the form, but maybe it's honest. Maybe the truest thing you can write in a book is not an insight but a reminder that you were a body in a room, needing things.

This is the thing about free writing: it drifts. You start with the bird on the fence and end up in the repair shop. That's not a failure; that's the shape of thought. Thought is not a train on a track, it's more like a walk through a neighborhood where you keep taking side streets because you heard music or smelled bread or remembered something you haven't thought about in ten years. The art is not in preventing the drift, but in noticing where the drift takes you and following it a little further than feels polite.

Let me follow it down one of those side streets. I want to talk about boredom.

Boredom has a bad reputation. We treat it like a moral failing, something to be solved with a phone, a podcast, a second screen while the first screen is still on. But I remember being bored as a kid in a way that felt enormous and generative. Summer afternoons when there was nowhere to go and nothing on. The heat made the air shimmer over the pavement. We would lie in the grass and look at the clouds until they stopped looking like anything and just became shapes. We would invent elaborate rules for games with no equipment. We would take apart a radio to see if we could put it back together. Usually we couldn't. The radio would stay in pieces on the kitchen table for a week, a monument to curiosity.

I don't think children are naturally more creative. I think they are more frequently bored, and boredom, properly allowed to sit, is a compost heap. It rots down all the assigned entertainment and leaves something richer. The mind, when not fed, starts to feed on itself in interesting ways. It makes connections it wouldn't otherwise make. It notices the way light falls. It hears the refrigerator hum. It starts to tell itself stories just to pass the time, and those stories are often truer than the ones we consume because they come from the one narrator we can't easily escape: ourselves, in an empty room.

I try to be bored on purpose now, which is a difficult discipline. I sit on a train without headphones. I take a walk without a destination or a podcast. I wash dishes and do not listen to anything. It's uncomfortable at first. The itch to check, to fill, to optimize is strong. But after ten minutes or so, something shifts. The mental commentary quiets. Details get sharper. I notice the weight of the plate in my hands, the pattern on the tile, the way the water beads. It is not mindfulness in the app-store sense. It's just being there long enough that there is nothing left to do but be there.

There's a writer I love who said that boredom is the state we need to be in to hear our own thoughts clearly. I think she was right, though I'd add that we also need to be in it to hear other people's thoughts clearly, disembarked from the noise of our own. When I'm bored, I'm less defensive. I can actually listen to a friend talk about their job, which they hate, without immediately drafting a solution. I can walk past a building I've walked past a hundred times and see the carved letters above the door that I've never read. Boredom returns us to the world as it is, not as we need it to be.

Speaking of worlds as they are — I have a weakness for maps. Not the digital kind that tell you where to go, but the old paper ones that tell you where you *are*, and also, implicitly, where you are not. I have a map of my city from 1978 folded in a drawer, soft as cloth from being opened and closed. The street names have changed. A whole neighborhood that used to be there is now a parking lot and a bank. Someone's grandfather walked those streets. My map does not know that, of course, but I know it when I look at it, and the two knowledges sit on top of each other like transparencies.

Maps lie, of course. They flatten. They choose. Every map is an argument about what matters. The subway map is a beautiful lie; it straightens curves and spaces stations evenly so that your journey feels rational. I love subway maps for that reason. They are designed to make a complicated system feel simple and navigable, which is a kindness. The real city is messier. It folds back on itself. You can walk in a straight line for ten minutes and end up exactly where you started because the street bends with the river. Paper maps admit this. They have creases where the city folds.

I think a lot about folding. How we fold our lives. We fold laundry, we fold letters, we fold ourselves into smaller shapes to fit into rooms, into jobs, into the expectations of people who love us and also, sometimes, people who don't know us at all. Some folds are soft, worn smooth from repeated use. Some are sharp, still hurting. The map in my drawer is a record of all my folds. You can tell where I lived by the creases. You can tell where I got lost by the worn spot where I kept refolding to find my bearings.

If this essay has a center, maybe it is that: the record of folds. The way we keep returning to certain places, certain phrases, certain stories, because the crease is already there and it makes the returning easier. I return to the same books. I return to the same walks. I return to the same questions in different years and get slightly different answers. It is not progress, exactly. It is more like circling, but the circle widens a little each time. Or maybe it's the same circle, but I am taller now and can see over the fence.

Let me try to be more concrete. Let me tell you about a Tuesday in March. I woke up early — not on purpose, just the way sleep sometimes ends — and the apartment was blue with that pre-dawn light that makes everything look underwater. I made coffee and stood by the window and watched a cat walk along the top of the back fence with the absolute confidence of an animal that has never once doubted its own balance. The cat stopped, looked back at me, and continued. I felt judged. I felt also, absurdly, inspired. I took that walk I mentioned, the one without a destination, and I ended up at the repair shop, where I did not need anything repaired. I stood there for a while looking at a bowl of keys that someone had left to be copied and never picked up. Whose keys were they? What doors did they open? I imagined a life for the owner, and then I imagined that my imagining was itself a kind of key, opening a door in me.

After the repair shop, I went to the library. I like libraries in the morning when they are quiet and the light comes in sideways. I like the smell of old paper and floor polish. I wandered the stacks without purpose, which is my favorite way to find a book. I pulled out a volume of essays by someone I had never heard of, published in 1962, and read the first paragraph by the window. It was about the pleasures of walking in the rain. The author said that rain on a walk was a form of attention: you cannot hurry, you cannot be distracted, you must look where you are going because there is water in your eyes. I have thought about that sentence for weeks. Rain as attention. I want to put that on a sign.

Later that Tuesday, I called my mother. We talked about nothing in particular, which is my favorite kind of talk. She told me about a dream she'd had in which she was trying to bake a cake but had forgotten how ovens worked. I told her about the cat on the fence. We laughed. After we hung up, I sat for a while with the phone in my hand, feeling the particular quiet that follows a good conversation. It is not empty. It is full in a different way, like a room after people have left a party still holding the warmth of bodies.

I am aware that I am risking the kind of essay that goes nowhere beautifully. But perhaps going nowhere beautifully is exactly what free writing is supposed to do. The assignment did not ask for a thesis. It asked for 2500 words about whatever I want. *Whatever I want* — that is a latitude, and latitudes are where the weather happens. I want to talk about small things that become large when you look at them long enough. I want to talk about weather more, actually, because weather is the most honest subject. It does not care what you think about it. It rains. It doesn't. It is too hot. It is too cold. It changes its mind every hour and never apologizes.

I have a theory that we prefer to talk about work, because work is legible. We can say what we did, how long it took, whether it succeeded. Weather is illegible. We can only say how it felt. We are embarrassed by feeling, so we make jokes about the weather instead. "Crazy weather we're having." It's a shield. But I think we talk about weather when we want to talk about how we are, and we don't know how to say that directly. "It's been a gray week" is not about the sky. It's about the Tuesday that started with blue light and ended with a phone call, and everything in between that was too small to name but too present to ignore.

Another small thing: I like the moment when a song ends and before the next one starts. That tiny silence. In a concert, you can feel it, the audience holding its breath together. At home, if you are listening to a record, you can hear the needle. I like that silence because it is a hinge. Everything before it is complete, everything after it is possible. Our lives are full of such hinges that we rush through. We end a conversation and immediately start another. We finish a book and pick up our phone. We arrive somewhere and already think about leaving. The hinge asks for a pause, just a second, just long enough to notice that you are between things, which is the only place you ever really are.

I could write a whole piece about hinges. The hinge of a door is a perfect metaphor, too perfect, which is why I distrust it. Doors are what we use to separate, but hinges are what make separation possible without destruction. You can close the door and still be connected to the room on the other side by that small, stubborn piece of metal. I think about that when I think about friendships that have gone quiet. The door is closed, but the hinge is still there. Maybe one day it will open again. Maybe it won't. Either way, the hinge remembers.

Let's talk about forgetting, since I've been circling it. Forgetting is not the opposite of memory. It's the partner. The brain is not a warehouse; it's an editor. It cuts. It keeps the highlights, the emotional centers, the one image that stands in for a whole day. I remember the way my grandmother's kitchen smelled, but I cannot remember the color of her walls. I remember that she hummed while she worked, but not what song. I remember a feeling of being held, which is more important than the color of the walls. Forgetting is how we make room for what matters. It is also how we distort. I am sure the kitchen was smaller than I remember, and also larger. Both are true in the way memories are true, which is to say, true to the person remembering.

I have started to keep a list of things I want to remember on purpose, because I know I will forget them otherwise. Not important things. Small things. The way the light hit the cat on the fence. The sentence about rain. The dream about the cake. My mother's laugh on the phone, which is the same laugh she has had since I was small, a sort of surprised bark. I write these down not because the list will preserve them, but because the act of choosing to remember is a kind of love. It says: this mattered to me. I will not let it slip. And if it does slip anyway, at least I tried to hold it.

There is a risk in that, of course. The risk of becoming a collector of moments instead of living through them. I have been guilty of watching a sunset through my phone screen, framing it instead of feeling it. But I have also learned that the list is not the enemy. The enemy is the belief that if you don't record it, it didn't count. It counted. It counts even if you forget the details. The feeling stays in the body long after the mind has moved on. I can feel that Tuesday in March in my shoulders, even if I forget the exact shade of blue.

And now, because free writing tends to find its own gravity, I find myself returning to the beginning. The blank page. The bird on the fence. The mug. The vertigo. Perhaps the freedom was not about choosing a topic but about learning to stay with whatever arrives and follow it until it surprises you. The repair shop surprised me. The library surprised me. Boredom surprised me. All of them were there all along, waiting for attention.

I want to end with something that is not an ending. Endings are difficult in free writing because nothing has been built to be concluded. There is no argument to wrap up, no story to resolve. So I will just stop in the middle of a thought, the way real life does. Real life does not end with a moral. It continues. The cat will come back to the fence tomorrow. The sparrow will defend its post. The keys in the bowl will stay unclaimed, or they won't. The tea will go cold again. And I, having written these words, will get up and make a new cup, and stand by the window, and watch the light do its thing on the wall, and for a little while, that will be enough.

There is more to say, obviously. There is always more to say. I could talk about the train I took once across the desert, how the land looked like an ocean that had forgotten how to move. I could talk about the man who sat across from me and ate an orange very slowly, peel in one piece, and how his hands were stained orange for the rest of the trip and he didn't seem to mind. I could talk about the letter I wrote when I was nineteen and never sent, which I still have in a drawer, and which begins "I don't know how to say this" — the most honest opening line ever invented. I could talk about names: how naming a thing changes it, how my grandmother called the spoon she used for soup "the good spoon" even though it was dented, and how that naming made it good.

I could talk about all of that, and maybe I will, some other day, in another blank space with another large number. For now, I have used up a good portion of my freedom just by wandering. If you have wandered with me this far, thank you. I hope you noticed something small along the way. I hope the hinge held.

The light is changing now. It's moving off the wall and onto the floor, where it will stay for a while before it leaves altogether. I should go and see where it lands.

I write these down not because the list will preserve them, but because the act of choosing to remember is a kind of love. It says: this mattered to me. I will not let it slip. And if it does slip anyway, at least I tried to hold it.

There is a risk in that, of course. The risk of becoming a collector of moments instead of living through them. I have been guilty of watching a sunset through my phone screen, framing it instead of feeling it. But I have also learned that the list is not the enemy. The enemy is the belief that if you don't record it, it didn't count. It counted. It counts even if you forget the details. The feeling stays in the body long after the mind has moved on. I can feel that Tuesday in March in my shoulders, even if I forget the exact shade of blue.

And now, because free writing tends to find its own gravity, I find myself returning to the beginning. The blank page. The bird on the fence. The mug. The vertigo. Perhaps the freedom was not about choosing a topic but about learning to stay with whatever arrives and follow it until it surprises you. The repair shop surprised me. The library surprised me. Boredom surprised me. All of them were there all along, waiting for attention.

I want to end with something that is not an ending. Endings are difficult in free writing because nothing has been built to be concluded. There is no argument to wrap up, no story to resolve. So I will just stop in the middle of a thought, the way real life does. Real life does not end with a moral. It continues. The cat will come back to the fence tomorrow. The sparrow will defend its post. The keys in the bowl will stay unclaimed, or they won't. The tea will go cold again. And I, having written these words, will get up and make a new cup, and stand by the window, and watch the light do its thing on the wall, and for a little while, that will be enough.

There is more to say, obviously. There is always more to say. I could talk about the train I took once across the desert, how the land looked like an ocean that had forgotten how to move. I could talk about the man who sat across from me and ate an orange very slowly, peel in one piece, and how his hands were stained orange for the rest of the trip and he didn't seem to mind. I could talk about the letter I wrote when I was nineteen and never sent, which I still have in a drawer, and which begins "I don't know how to say this" — the most honest opening line ever invented. I could talk about names: how naming a thing changes it, how my grandmother called the spoon she used for soup "the good spoon" even though it was dented, and how that naming made it good.

I could talk about all of that, and maybe I will, some other day, in another blank space with another large number. For now, I have used up a good portion of my freedom just by wandering. If you have wandered with me this far, thank you. I hope you noticed something small along the way. I hope the hinge held.

The light is changing now. It's moving off the wall and onto the floor, where it will stay for a while before it leaves altogether. I should go and see where it lands.
